title: Continual Learning Has Quietly Moved Outside the Weights
hook: Classical continual learning was about updating weights without forgetting. This survey argues the field has moved to system-level adaptation — memory, skill libraries, harnesses.
key_points: Classical continual learning is parameter-centric: training strategies, architectures, and weight adaptation.
Newer paradigms break that frame — on-policy learning widens the update mechanisms available.
Test-time training extends continual learning from the training phase into inference.
External harness components — memory, skill libraries, interaction protocols — extend capability beyond the static parameter space.
The survey organizes the shift along three axes: When learning happens, How it happens, and Where it lands.
Where is the sharpest axis: updates to internal parameters versus updates to external structure.
content_html: Continual learning used to have a crisp definition: keep updating a model's parameters on new data without destroying what it already knew. Hou and colleagues argue that definition no longer describes what practitioners are actually doing, and offer a survey organized around the shift.
extra_html:
Three axes

The framing is tri-axial. How covers the update mechanics — off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient methods. When covers the stage at which learning happens, now spanning pre-training, post-training, and inference time. Where is the axis that carries the argument: updates can land in internal parameters, or in external structure entirely.

That last axis is where the transition shows. Test-time training pushes adaptation into inference. Agent harnesses accumulate memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols that expand what a system can do while its weights sit frozen. Read together, the authors say, these developments mark a move from parameter-centric learning to system-level adaptation — and the survey uses the framework to place representative methods and to name the open problems the shift creates.

related.title: Agentic Test-Time Training: Adapting Mid-Episode
related.hook: LLM agents degrade over long episodes, repeating failed moves — this method updates the model's weights continuously during the episode itself, but only on genuinely new information.

related.title: Agents That Learn on the Job Without Weight Updates
related.hook: An agent that cracks a hard request today starts from zero tomorrow. Distil each episode into a retrievable rule and a frozen model gets 2.6x better — no fine-tuning.

related.title: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation
related.hook: Most agent-optimization papers report a one-shot gain and stop. Rerun the optimizer on new tasks and two of three popular methods actually make the agent worse than doing nothing.

flashcards.prompt: What are the three axes this survey uses to characterize continual learning?
flashcards.back_html: When learning occurs (pre-training, post-training, inference-time), How it occurs (off-policy, on-policy, beyond-gradient), and Where the update lands (internal parameters versus external structure).

flashcards.prompt: What transition does the survey argue continual learning is undergoing?

choices.text: From parameter-centric model adaptation toward system-level adaptation
From supervised objectives toward purely self-supervised ones
From small specialist models toward a single general model per domain

flashcards.explanation_html: The claim is that mechanisms like test-time training and external harness components — memory, skill libraries, interaction protocols — now extend a system's capabilities without touching the static parameter space at all.

flashcards.prompt: Give two examples of learning that happens outside a model's weights.
flashcards.back_html: Test-time training, which moves adaptation into the inference phase, and external harness components such as memory stores, skill libraries, and interaction protocols that grow capability without weight updates.
